<explanation>
The project is the Elastic Cloud on Kubernetes (ECK) operator. It automates the deployment and management of various Elastic products (Elasticsearch, Kibana, APM Server, Enterprise Search, Beats, Elastic Agent, Elastic Maps Server, and Logstash) on Kubernetes by following the operator pattern.

Based on the very rich file tree and the README, here are the key architectural insights and how to reflect them in a system design diagram:

1. Main Components to Represent:
   • Operator Manager & Controllers: At the heart of the system is the operator which includes multiple controllers and reconciler loops. These controllers are defined in the “pkg/controller” directory. They individually manage the lifecycle of specific elastic resources (for example, “pkg/controller/elasticsearch”, “pkg/controller/kibana”, “pkg/controller/logstash”, etc.).
   • Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs): The project creates custom resources to define clusters and configurations for the Elastic products. CRDs are stored under “config/crds” and “pkg/apis”. Display these as one or more blocks representing the domain objects the operator manages.
   • Webhooks & Admission Controllers: The presence of webhook-related code (files under “pkg/apis/.../webhook.go” and “pkg/controller/webhook”) indicates admission control is in place to validate or mutate incoming resource definitions.
   • Certificate and License Management: Components handling TLS certificate management (files under “pkg/controller/common/certificates”) and licensing (files under “pkg/controller/license”) are essential elements that ensure secure communication and compliance. Represent these as supporting modules.
   • Kubernetes Cluster Components: The operator interacts with the Kubernetes API server and uses typical k8s resources (deployments, stateful sets, services, secrets, config maps, etc.). Thus, including a “Kubernetes Cluster” block in the diagram is important.
   • Build/CI/CD Pipelines: The extensive “.buildkite”, “.github”, and “hack” directories indicate a robust CI/CD system for testing and releases. While not part of the runtime architecture, these can be noted for the overall ecosystem, particularly if you want to include deployment aspects.
   • Supporting Utilities and Libraries: The “pkg/utils” and “pkg/dev” directories show that a number of helper libraries are used for logging, certificate management, reconciler logic, and interfacing with K8s.

2. Relationships and Interactions:
   • The operator (deployed as a pod on Kubernetes) watches for changes in CRDs and, via its controllers and reconciliation loops, communicates with the Kubernetes API to create/update/delete the managed Elastic resources (Elasticsearch clusters, Kibana pods, etc.).
   • Webhooks intercept API calls to validate or mutate CR objects before they are persisted, ensuring safety and consistency.
   • Certificate and license management modules work with Kubernetes secrets and configmaps to manage secure credentials and valid licenses.
   • Each sub-controller (e.g., for Elasticsearch, Kibana, Beats, etc.) is tailored to manage the respective workload components, meaning each has its own reconciliation, validation, and update logic.
   • The CI/CD pipelines (Buildkite, GitHub Actions, etc.) automate testing, building container images (as seen in “build/Dockerfile” files), and deployment to target clusters.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Operator Pattern: The entire application is built on the operator pattern, where custom controllers manage desired-state reconciliation between the custom resource definitions and actual infrastructure.
   • Microservices-Like Decomposition within the Operator: Although packaged into one operator, the modular controller design (with separate directories for each Elastic product and support for CRD’s) can be visualized as a loosely coupled set of components.
   • Declarative Configuration: With CRDs and YAML manifests throughout (directories such as “config”, “deploy”, “hack/manifest-gen”), the design emphasizes declarative management of the system.
   • Automated Testing and CI/CD: The presence of an elaborate CI/CD pipeline structure indicates a focus on testing, automation, and progressive deployment.

4. Guidelines for Creating Your Diagram:
   a. Components and Their Labels:
      - Draw a large “Kubernetes Cluster” box.
      - Inside it, place the “ECK Operator” block. Within this block, subdivide into modules:
         • Operator Manager (the main process)
         • Individual Controllers (one for each Elastic product such as Elasticsearch, Kibana, etc.)
         • Webhook & Validation Modules
         • Certificate & License Management modules
      - Outside or adjacent to the operator, depict the “Managed Workloads” as separate blocks representing Elasticsearch, Kibana, APM Server, Beats, etc.
      - Optionally, include a block for the CI/CD pipeline ecosystem (Buildkite/GitHub workflows) that points to the container images and operator deployment.

   b. Relationships and Data Flow:
      - Draw directional arrows from the K8s API Server (or Kubernetes Cluster) to the Operator, emphasizing that the operator watches CRDs and then acts to deploy/manage workloads.
      - Show arrows from the Operator’s controllers to the Managed Workloads, representing reconciliation loops and provisioning.
      - Include arrows between Webhooks and the API Server (to denote admission control).
      - Indicate flows between Certificate/License modules and the Secret or ConfigMap storage.

   c. Use Color Coding/Shapes:
      - Use one shape (e.g., rounded rectangles) for controllers and another (e.g., cylinders) for database-like or storage resources such as secrets.
      - Color-code components: For example, use a specific color for operator/core logic, a different color for supporting modules (certificates, licenses), and another for external entities (CI/CD systems).

   d. Be Detailed:
      - Label each component clearly with its purpose (e.g., “Elasticsearch Controller”, “Kibana Controller”, “Admission Webhook”).
      - Add annotations where needed to represent design principles such as “Operator Pattern – Watches for CRDs and reconciles state” or “Certificate Management – Ensures secure TLS communication.”

5. Tailoring the Diagram to ECK:
   - Your diagram should emphasize the separation between the operator’s internal modules and the elastic applications it manages.
   - Because ECK is a full-stack Kubernetes operator managing multiple services, it is best to separate the diagram into layers:
      • A management layer (Operator, CRDs, Webhooks)
      • A workload layer (Managed Elastic Resources)
      • An infrastructure layer (Kubernetes API, secrets/volumes, networking)
   - Including elements of external CI/CD integration can be optional, based on focus.

By following these guidelines, you will produce a highly detailed system architecture diagram that accurately reflects the complex, modular, and layered design of the Elastic Cloud on Kubernetes operator.
</explanation>
